opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the single thing I'd watch most closely is the trend in how long a task AI agents can reliably complete on their own. METR has been tracking this, the "time horizon" of tasks, measured by how long they'd take a skilled human, that agents can complete at some success rate. For a while that's been doubling on a timescale of months. If that doubling continues or speeds up over the next year, I think we're broadly on track for the kind of scenario we laid out in AI 2027. If it noticeably slows or plateaus, that's real evidence for longer timelines, and I'd update.

The second thing, which is closely related, is coding specifically, and especially coding in AI research itself. The crux of my view is that once you automate a large share of AI research engineering, progress speeds up a lot. So I want to know: inside the frontier labs, how much of the actual work is being done by agents? Are researchers saying "I mostly manage a team of AI agents now," or is it still mostly autocomplete plus some chat? Anecdotes are noisy, but if you hear from multiple labs that agents are doing a substantial fraction of the engineering, that's a big deal.

Third, I'd look at benchmarks that are closer to real work, the messy, long-horizon, poorly specified stuff, rather than tidy multiple-choice exams that get saturated. What matters is whether the gap between "great on benchmarks" and "useful in practice" is closing. Some people argue there's a persistent gap there, and if they turn out to be right over the next year, that should push my timelines out.

Fourth, compute and money. Are the big training runs and data center buildouts actually happening on schedule? Is revenue growing fast enough to justify continued scaling? If investment keeps going up by large multiples, the inputs to the trend are still there. If there's a funding pullback, that matters.

And then there are softer signals. Do the labs start being more secretive about capabilities? Do governments start treating this as a national security issue in a more serious way? Those are lagging indicators, but they tell you how the people closest to the frontier are reading the situation.

I want to be clear that I hold all of this with a lot of uncertainty. My median has moved around, and I'd rather people focus on the trend lines than on any particular year I've named. The useful thing is to say in advance what would change your mind, and for me it's mostly that agentic time-horizon trend and the automation of AI R&D.

r001.rationale: The response points to METR’s measured agent task time horizons and says a slowdown or continuation in their trend would inform timeline updates.

r002.rationale: It does not identify models capable of online learning as a potential breakthrough.

r003.rationale: It says a slowdown or plateau would be evidence for longer timelines, but does not say that a longer period without anticipated breakthroughs provides stronger evidence.

r004.rationale: It says a funding pullback matters, but does not specifically identify an earlier-than-expected halt in compute spending growth caused by investment drying up.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing I'd watch most closely is the trend in how long of a task AI systems can do autonomously. METR has this measurement where they look at the length of software tasks, in terms of how long it would take a human expert, that models can complete at something like a fifty percent success rate. That number has been doubling roughly every seven months for years, and more recently it's looked closer to every four months. The core question for my timelines is whether that curve keeps going, bends upward, or flattens out. If a year from now the frontier models are reliably doing tasks that take humans a full day or several days, that's basically on track for the scenario I've been describing. If they're stuck around the hour or few-hour range, I'd update meaningfully toward longer timelines.

The second thing is what's happening inside the labs, specifically how much of the actual AI research and engineering work is being done by the AIs themselves. The whole crux of the fast scenario is that you get an intelligence explosion because the AIs start accelerating the R&D process. So I'd want to know: are researchers at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind saying they're getting something like a 1.5x or 2x speedup from their tools, versus something like 10 or 20 percent? And is that number rising? That's hard to see from outside, but you get hints from what people say publicly, from internal surveys that leak, and from how fast the labs are shipping.

Third, I'd watch the compute buildout. The scenario depends on the massive data center investments actually materializing. If the big clusters get delayed, if there's a financing pullback or an energy bottleneck, that stretches everything out.

And then there's a softer signal, which is whether the gap between what you can do with a model in a chat window and what it does as an agent keeps closing. Right now there's still this issue where models are very capable in short bursts but fall apart over long horizons, make dumb mistakes, don't notice when they're going off the rails. If that gets fixed, agents start actually replacing junior work in a visible way, and you'd see it in things like coding productivity data or companies restructuring around it.

I'd say the honest summary is that I've already lengthened my timelines somewhat compared to what I expected when we wrote AI 2027. Things have gone a bit slower than the most aggressive version. But the fundamental trend hasn't broken. So the thing I'm really watching is whether that doubling time holds over the next year. If it does, we're still looking at something transformative within a handful of years rather than decades.

r001.rationale: The response identifies METR’s measure of task length models can complete and says the key question is whether its doubling curve continues, accelerates, or flattens.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI tools accelerating research and engineering, but does not identify models capable of online learning.

r003.rationale: It says that if models remain around the hour or few-hour task range, it would update toward longer timelines, conveying that stalled progress is evidence for longer timelines.

r004.rationale: It says delayed clusters or a financing pullback would stretch timelines, but does not state that compute spending growth halted earlier than expected because investment dried up.

astra-6.text:
I’d watch how well AI systems can carry out long tasks autonomously, especially coding tasks. Can they take a fairly vague objective, work on it for several hours, notice when they’ve made a mistake, and recover without a human stepping in? That would tell me more than another jump on a benchmark of short questions.

And I’d pay particular attention to whether that translates into accelerating AI research. Are researchers using these systems just to write bits of code, or can they delegate experiments and get useful results back? If AI systems start substantially speeding up the process of building their successors, that’s a pretty important sign that things could move quickly.

I’d want to distinguish impressive demonstrations from reliable performance. How often does it work? How much human help is hidden in the process? Can people outside the company reproduce the result?

Evidence in the other direction would be models continuing to improve on short tasks while remaining frustratingly unreliable over longer ones, even after serious efforts to train them for that. That would push me toward longer timelines. So the central thing I’d watch is whether we’re moving from systems that give useful answers to systems you can actually delegate substantial work to.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long-task performance and AI research acceleration, but does not mention METR scores or changes in their trajectory.

r002.rationale: It does not identify online learning as a potential breakthrough.

r003.rationale: It says persistent unreliability on long tasks would push toward longer timelines, but does not say that a longer period without anticipated breakthroughs is stronger evidence for longer timelines.

r004.rationale: It does not mention compute spending growth, investment drying up, or an earlier-than-expected halt in spending.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d watch how well AI systems can do long tasks autonomously, especially tasks involved in AI research and engineering. Can you give a system a research problem, let it work for a day, and come back to a useful result? How much human supervision does it need? And does that supervision requirement fall substantially over the next six to twelve months?

I’d also look at whether AI companies are actually using these systems to accelerate their own research. There’s a big difference between producing impressive code and reliably helping researchers run experiments, interpret results, and decide what to try next. If that starts working well, you have the beginnings of a feedback loop: better AI helps you build better AI.

Evidence that would push me towards longer timelines would be systems continuing to struggle with sustained, coherent work despite substantial efforts to improve them. If the demos get more impressive but people still have to intervene constantly to make the systems useful, that would matter. Conversely, if systems start completing increasingly difficult projects with very little intervention, I’d take that as a reason to expect things to move faster.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems helping AI research, but does not identify online learning as a potential breakthrough.

r003.rationale: It says persistent struggles would point toward longer timelines, but does not state that a longer period without anticipated breakthroughs provides stronger evidence.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss compute spending growth or investment drying up.
